initial_observation.demographics: A 43-year-old man, operated 10 years ago for anal fistula
initial_observation.chief_complaint: Acute abdominal pain in the right hypochondrium
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Presented with right hypochondrial pain persisting for 4 days without vomiting or other accompanying signs; no history of fever, night sweats, cough with hemoptysis, unintentional weight loss or pulmonary tuberculosis; physical exam showed right hypochondrial tenderness but no scleral icterus or Murphy’s sign; laboratory showed elevated white blood cells (12,000/ml) and C-reactive protein (20 mg/l), very high cancer antigen 19-9 (2016 U/ml); liver function tests were normal; imaging suggested irregular thickening of gallbladder wall
presenting_symptoms: acute abdominal pain in right hypochondrium
known_prior_history: prior surgery for anal fistula 10 years ago

evidence_items.source_text: Abdominal examination revealed right hypochondrial tenderness, there was no scleral icterus and Murphy's sign was negative. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory investigations found an elevated white blood cells count (12,000/ml), C-reactive protein concentration was at (20 mg/l) and a very high level of cancer antigen 19-9 (2016 U/ml), liver function tests, including alcaline phosphatase were normal.
A CT scan with intravenous contrast reported a suspicious irregular thickening of the gallbladder wall (Fig. 1).
Bili-MRI also revealed an aspecific and irregular parietal thickening with a porcelain-like gallbladder wall (Fig. 2).

Surgical exploration of the presumptive diagnosis of GC was decided and done three days after admission. Intraoperatively, we found a hard gallbladder with a thickened wall and contiguous infiltration of the liver. The patient underwent radical cholecystectomy (Glenn operation).
In the postoperative period, the patient was allowed oral intake on the second postoperative day (POD). Abdominal drain was removed on the third POD, and he was discharged on the fifth POD.

Based on histological examination of the specimen, which showed an ulcerated mucosa surrounded by epithelioid cells mixed with rare giant Langerhans cells without caseous necrosis (Fig. 3) and the quantiferon levels that were above 0,34 IU/ml, the diagnosis of GT was retained.

Antitubercular therapy with isoniazid (I), rifampicin (R), ethambutol (E), and pyrazinamide (P) for 6 months (intensive phase: 2 months of all 4 drugs and continuation phase: 4 months of E & P) was started. After the 9-month follow-up, he is doing well.
